Fetal Echo Project · Unit D11 · Detect tier · v0.2

When and how to refer

DRAFT - NOT FOR CLINICAL USE. Contains claims with status 'ai-extracted' that no clinician has verified.

You will be able to

  • Apply the basic rule: a fetus with a suspected abnormality on screening is a candidate for fetal echocardiography.
  • List the fetal findings that are indications for fetal echocardiography.
  • List the maternal and family factors that are indications.
  • Tell apart factors where echocardiography may be considered and factors with insufficient evidence.
  • Say who should perform the fetal echocardiogram and what counselling should take into account.

The basic rule

A fetus with a known or suspected abnormality on cardiac screening is a candidate for fetal echocardiography.1

The echocardiography guideline says the same from its side: fetal echocardiography is indicated when the screening ultrasound of the heart is abnormal, whether or not there are other risk factors.2

A low threshold for referral is one of the measures that can improve a screening programme.3

You do not need to name the lesion: suspicion on an adequate view is enough. A view that could not be obtained is a different situation. With an unfavourable fetal lie, extra examination time or a second examination may be needed.1,4

Risk factors add to screening; they do not replace it

When there is a significant risk factor for congenital heart disease, fetal echocardiography is indicated in addition to routine screening, depending on local resources, the setting, the availability of examiners and the screening results.5

A high proportion of detectable heart disease occurs in pregnancies with no risk factor and no extracardiac anomaly. This is why quality screening and timely referral matter.6

Fetal indications

The guideline lists these fetal factors as common indications for fetal echocardiography.7,8

Fetal factorDetail
Suspected structural anomaly of the heart
Extracardiac structural anomalyWith a known association with congenital heart disease
Suspected abnormal function or a large heart
Hydrops
Persistent tachycardia180 beats per minute or more
Suspected heart block
Persistent bradycardia110 beats per minute or less
Irregular rhythmFrequent or persistent
Increased nuchal translucency3.5 mm or more at 11 to 14 weeks
Genetic abnormalityConfirmed or suspected
Monochorionic twinsIf resources allow

A nuchal translucency of 3.5 mm or more at 11 to 14 weeks remains an indication even if the measurement later becomes normal.8

Findings on the screen that should not be passed

Right-left asymmetry of the ventricles in mid-gestation warrants further examination. Important causes are coarctation of the aorta, an evolving hypoplastic left heart and anomalous pulmonary venous return.9

A major difference in size between the two great arteries should lead to further evaluation.10

An abnormal cardiac axis raises the risk of a cardiac malformation, especially of the outflow tracts, and may be associated with a chromosomal anomaly.11

If the heart or the stomach is not on the left, suspect a situs abnormality.12

Maternal and family indications

The guideline lists these maternal, family and exposure factors as common indications.13

FactorDetail
Congenital heart disease in a first-degree relative of the fetusParents, siblings and half-siblings
Mendelian disease with childhood cardiac manifestationsIn a first- or second-degree relative
Pregestational diabetesWhatever the HbA1c
Anti-Ro/SSA antibodies
PhenylketonuriaUnknown status, or periconceptional phenylalanine above 10 mg/dL
Retinoid exposure
Confirmed fetal infectionTORCH or parvovirus B19

May be considered

For some factors the guideline says fetal echocardiography may be considered.14

FactorDetail
Congenital heart disease in a second-degree relative
Gestational diabetesDiagnosed in the first or early second trimester
Nuchal translucency3.0 to 3.4 mm
Selected teratogensFor example paroxetine, carbamazepine, lithium, sodium valproate
Conception by IVFIncluding ICSI
ACE inhibitor use

Not enough evidence of raised risk

For each of these factors, taken on its own, the guideline finds insufficient evidence that the risk of congenital heart disease is significantly above baseline.15

FactorDetail
ObesityBMI 35 kg/m2 or more
SSRI exposureOther than paroxetine
Non-cardiac soft markersFor aneuploidy
Abnormal serum analytes
Single umbilical arteryIsolated
Gestational diabetesDiagnosed after the second trimester
Warfarin or alcohol exposure
Echogenic intracardiac focus
Prenatal fever, or viral infection with seroconversion only
Congenital heart disease in a distant relativeIsolated; more distant than second degree

This is a statement about the factor alone. A suspected abnormality on the screen makes the fetus a candidate for fetal echocardiography whatever the history, and a significant risk factor that is also present still counts.1,5

These pregnancies have the same routine cardiac screen as every other: situs, four-chamber view, outflow tracts and great-vessel views.16

How the echocardiography guideline compares

The American echocardiography guideline has its own table of indications. Most entries agree with the screening guideline. The points below are where its wording adds something.

It lists as indications: pregestational diabetes, maternal SSA/SSB antibodies, congenital heart disease in a first-degree relative, hydrops, an extracardiac anomaly, monochorionic twins, and a nuchal translucency of 3.5 mm or more.17,18,19,20,21,22,23

After IVF, or with a nuchal translucency of 3.0 to 3.4 mm, it says fetal echocardiography may be considered, and that after a normal cardiac screen the decision should take the accuracy of local screening into account.24,25

An isolated single umbilical artery does not by itself indicate fetal echocardiography when the second-trimester cardiac screen is normal.26

Who does the echocardiogram, and what families need

Fetal echocardiography is best performed by a trained specialist who is familiar with prenatal diagnosis and with the course, management and prognosis after birth.27

Counselling after a heart problem is detected should take into account the high prevalence of psychological distress in the mother.27

Findings on the three-vessel views can change what happens next: testing for 22q11 microdeletion, the planned place of delivery as in complete transposition, readiness to give prostaglandin, or readiness for airway problems from vascular compression.28

Before you close the report: common reasons to refer (not a complete list)

  • Suspected cardiac abnormality on any plane. (A view that could not be obtained is an incomplete scan: more time or a second examination.)1,4
  • Rate stays at 110 or below, or at 180 or above; suspected heart block; frequent or persistently irregular rhythm7
  • Ventricles asymmetric in mid-gestation: further examination. Major difference in size between the great arteries: further evaluation9,10
  • Heart or stomach not on the left: suspect a situs abnormality. Abnormal axis: raised risk of a cardiac malformation12,11
  • Extracardiac structural anomaly known to go with heart disease; hydrops; confirmed or suspected genetic abnormality; monochorionic twins if resources allow7
  • Nuchal translucency was 3.5 mm or more at 11 to 14 weeks, even if it later became normal8
  • Maternal or family indication: check the full table in this unit (examples: congenital heart disease in a parent, sibling or half-sibling; pregestational diabetes; anti-Ro/SSA antibodies)13
